intro: Every text in this file is public domain. Nothing is reproduced from a modern copyrighted translation.

SOURCES World English Bible with Deuterocanon (eBible.org) - public domain dedication. Old and New Testaments, full deuterocanon, wider Orthodox canon. 37,874 verses across 81 books. R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch, 1917 - 108 chapters. R. H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees, 1917 - 50 chapters. Ante-Nicene Fathers vols. 1, 2, 7, 8, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885 - Apostolic Fathers, Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, New Testament apocrypha, Shepherd of Hermas. Roberts-Donaldson shorter recension, 1885 - seven genuine Ignatian letters.

ORDER Sections I-X run by date of composition, not canonical order. The file opens with the Song of the Sea, not Genesis 1; Genesis sits in Section V. Sections 12-16 hold the extra-canonical collections.

NOT PRESENT, AND WHY The Dead Sea Scrolls appear as summaries. Every English translation of the 1947+ finds is under copyright, and the Hebrew and Aramaic exists as photographs rather than machine-readable transcription. Psalms of Solomon and Philo are public domain but survive only as OCR of critical editions where translation and footnotes share every column. 1 Clement breaks off at chapter 59 and Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans lacks chapter 13. Both are holes in the 1885 printing this was scraped from, not in the public domain: the 1870 Ante-Nicene Christian Library closed the Hermas and Papias gaps, but it predates the 1873 discovery of the Jerusalem manuscript that carries the rest of 1 Clement.

sections.title: SECTION I.  EARLIEST IDENTIFIABLE MATERIAL
sections.name: EARLIEST IDENTIFIABLE MATERIAL
intro: Two archaic Hebrew poems are widely regarded as the oldest continuous literary units preserved in the Bible. Linguistically they look older than the prose that now surrounds them, and most critical scholars place them in the 12th-11th centuries BCE or shortly after. Both celebrate deliverance in battle; both were later embedded in much larger narrative books, which is why they appear again in their canonical position later in this volume.

works.title: THE SONG OF THE SEA (Exodus 15)
note: Victory hymn after the crossing of the sea. Verse 21, the couplet attributed to Miriam, is often treated as the oldest fragment of all. The full book of Exodus appears in Section V.

works.title: THE SONG OF DEBORAH (Judges 5)
note: A poetic account of the defeat of Sisera, older than the prose version in Judges 4 that now precedes it. The full book of Judges appears in Section III.

works.title: ALSO OFTEN DATED THIS EARLY
note: Other units frequently assigned to the same horizon, though with less agreement: the Blessing of Jacob (Genesis 49), the Oracles of Balaam (Numbers 23-24), the Blessing of Moses (Deuteronomy 33), and Psalm 68. Each appears in this volume within its canonical book.

On the Torah as a whole: traditional Jewish and Christian teaching assigns it to Moses in the 15th-13th century BCE. Critical scholarship assigns the final literary form to the Persian period. This volume follows the critical framework of the source guide and places the Torah in Section V, with Deuteronomy in Section III. That is an editorial decision about arrangement, not a claim about the antiquity of the traditions inside those books, much of which is older than the books themselves.

sections.title: SECTION II.  EIGHTH-CENTURY PROPHETIC BOOKS
sections.name: EIGHTH-CENTURY PROPHETIC BOOKS
intro: The earliest prophetic books whose core oracles can be dated with relative confidence. All four address the same world: prosperous, unequal kingdoms living in the shadow of Assyrian expansion. Their common themes are social injustice, covenant infidelity, and judgment that arrives through imperial politics. All are in every major canon.

works.title: AMOS
note: Active c. 760-750 BCE in the northern kingdom, though from Tekoa in Judah. The oldest prophetic book. Its center is the charge that ritual observance cannot substitute for justice.

positions.tradWhy: The book names its prophet and dates him by two reigns.
positions.crit: Amos, c. 760-750 BCE, with later editorial additions
positions.critWhy: The core oracles are accepted as genuinely his; the closing promise of restoration is often judged a later addition.
positions.critSource: Amos 9:11-15; Wellhausen, Die kleinen Propheten, 1892

works.title: HOSEA
note: Northern kingdom, c. 750-725 BCE, up to the eve of Samaria's fall. Frames the covenant as a marriage and infidelity as adultery.

positions.tradWhy: Named and dated in the book's opening verse.
positions.crit: Hosea, 8th century BCE, with later Judean editing
positions.critWhy: References to Judah in a northern prophet's book are widely taken as southern additions.
positions.critSource: Hosea 1:1, 1:7; Wellhausen, Die kleinen Propheten, 1892

works.title: ISAIAH 1-39 (FIRST ISAIAH)
note: Jerusalem, c. 740-700 BCE, spanning the Syro-Ephraimite crisis and Sennacherib's invasion of 701. Chapters 40-55 and 56-66 are the work of later hands and appear in Sections IV and V. Chapters 24-27 and 34-35 are also usually dated later than the eighth century.

positions.trad: Isaiah son of Amoz wrote the whole book, 8th century BCE
positions.tradWhy: The book is one scroll under one name. Ben Sira, writing c. 180 BCE, already credits the single prophet Isaiah with comforting the mourners of Zion, which is the language of chapter 40 onward. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran carries all 66 chapters continuously.
positions.tradSource: Sirach 48:22-25, in this volume; 1QIsa-a (Qumran, 2nd century BCE); Isaiah 1:1
positions.critWhy: Chapters 1-39 address the 8th-century Assyrian crisis; from chapter 40 the audience is in Babylonian exile 150 years later, with different vocabulary and theology.
positions.critSource: J. C. Doderlein, 1775; Bernhard Duhm, Das Buch Jesaia, 1892

works.title: MICAH
note: A contemporary of Isaiah from the Judean countryside. Chapters 1-3 are the securely eighth- century core; later material has been added.

sections.title: SECTION III.  SEVENTH CENTURY AND DEUTERONOMIC ACTIVITY
sections.name: SEVENTH CENTURY AND DEUTERONOMIC ACTIVITY
intro: The century of Assyrian decline, Josiah's reform, Babylonian ascent, and the fall of Jerusalem. The core of Deuteronomy is usually connected to the law book found in the temple in 622 BCE. The long historical work running from Joshua through Kings, shaped by Deuteronomy's outlook, takes form in this period and receives its final edition during the exile.

works.title: DEUTERONOMY
note: Presented as Moses' farewell addresses. The legal core, roughly chapters 12-26, is commonly linked to Josiah's reform of 622 BCE, with earlier material inside it and exilic framing around it. It is placed here rather than with the other four books of the Torah because of that link; see the note in Section V.

positions.tradWhy: Presented as Moses' farewell addresses; the book describes him writing the law and entrusting it to the Levites.
positions.crit: 7th century BCE, connected to Josiah's reform of 622
positions.critWhy: The law book found in the temple matches Deuteronomy's distinctive demand for a single sanctuary, and its style differs sharply from the rest of the Torah.
positions.critSource: W. M. L. de Wette, 1805; the correspondence is with 2 Kings 22:8-23:25

works.title: ZEPHANIAH
note: Judah, shortly before or during Josiah's reform. The day of the LORD as universal reckoning.

works.title: NAHUM
note: On the fall of Nineveh, 612 BCE. Composed shortly before or after that event.

works.title: HABAKKUK
note: Late seventh century, as Babylon rises. Asks why God uses a crueler nation to punish a bad one. The pesher on this book from Qumran is described in Section VII.

works.title: JEREMIAH
note: Career from c. 627 to after 586 BCE, so the book straddles this section and the exile. Preserved in two significantly different editions: the shorter Greek text and the longer Hebrew text translated here. Both forms are attested at Qumran.

positions.trad: Jeremiah, dictated to his scribe Baruch
positions.tradWhy: The book describes exactly that process, twice.
positions.critWhy: The Greek text is about an eighth shorter and differently ordered, showing the book still circulated in more than one form. Qumran preserves fragments of both.
positions.critSource: 4QJer-b (short form) and 4QJer-a (long form); Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 1992

works.title: JOSHUA
note: Deuteronomistic History, part 1. Conquest and land allotment.

positions.trad: Joshua, with a later hand for the account of his death
positions.tradWhy: The Talmud assigns the book to Joshua himself.
positions.crit: Part of the Deuteronomistic History, 7th-6th century BCE
positions.critWhy: Shares the language and theology of Deuteronomy, and the recurring phrase 'to this day' implies a much later vantage.
positions.critSource: Martin Noth, Uberlieferungsgeschichtliche Studien, 1943

works.title: JUDGES
note: Deuteronomistic History, part 2. Contains the archaic Song of Deborah reproduced in Section I.

positions.tradWhy: The Talmud assigns Judges to Samuel.
positions.crit: Deuteronomistic History, 7th-6th century BCE, around older material
positions.critWhy: The Song of Deborah in chapter 5 is archaic Hebrew, older than the prose account of the same events in chapter 4.
positions.critSource: Noth, 1943; on the antiquity of chapter 5, Albright, 1936

works.title: 1 SAMUEL
note: Deuteronomistic History, part 3. Includes older source material on Saul and David.

positions.trad: Samuel, continued by the prophets Nathan and Gad
positions.tradWhy: Chronicles names records kept by Samuel, Nathan and Gad, and the Talmud builds its attribution on that.
positions.critWhy: Samuel dies partway through the book that bears his name.
positions.critSource: Noth, 1943; 1 Samuel 25:1

works.title: 2 SAMUEL
note: Deuteronomistic History, part 4. Chapters 9-20 with 1 Kings 1-2 form the so-called Succession Narrative, often judged among the oldest sustained Hebrew prose.

positions.trad: Nathan and Gad, Samuel having died
positions.tradWhy: The Talmud continues the attribution to the surviving prophets.
positions.critWhy: The Succession Narrative in chapters 9-20 is regarded by many as among the oldest sustained prose in the Bible, later incorporated into the larger work.
positions.critSource: Leonhard Rost, Die Uberlieferung von der Thronnachfolge Davids, 1926

works.title: 1 KINGS
note: Deuteronomistic History, part 5.

positions.tradWhy: The Talmud assigns Kings to Jeremiah.
positions.crit: Deuteronomistic History; a first edition under Josiah, a second in exile
positions.critWhy: The book cites royal annals as its sources and carries the story into the exile.
positions.critSource: Frank Moore Cross, Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic, 1973, revising Noth's single-exilic model

works.title: 2 KINGS
note: Deuteronomistic History, part 6. Ends in 561 BCE with Jehoiachin released in Babylon, which sets the earliest possible date for the final edition.

positions.tradWhy: The Talmud assigns Kings to Jeremiah.
positions.crit: Deuteronomistic History, completed in exile after 561 BCE
positions.critWhy: It ends with Jehoiachin's release from prison, an event dated to 561, which the book cannot precede.

sections.title: SECTION IV.  THE EXILIC PERIOD
sections.name: THE EXILIC PERIOD
intro: Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed, the leadership is deported, and the literature turns to lament, explanation, and the possibility of return. Much earlier legal and historical material is edited during these decades.

works.title: EZEKIEL
note: A priest deported in 597, active c. 593-571 BCE in Babylonia. Combines priestly law with visionary imagery: the chariot throne, the glory departing and returning, the valley of dry bones, and a blueprint temple in chapters 40-48.

positions.trad: Ezekiel the priest, in exile, 593-571 BCE
positions.tradWhy: The book is precisely dated throughout and written in the first person.
positions.tradSource: Ezekiel 1:1-3, and the fourteen dated oracles thereafter
positions.crit: Ezekiel, 593-571 BCE, with a later editorial school
positions.critWhy: Its internal dates are unusually consistent, and the critical and traditional positions sit closer here than almost anywhere else in the prophets.
positions.critSource: Walther Zimmerli, Ezechiel, 1969

works.title: LAMENTATIONS
note: Five poems on the destruction of 587 BCE. Four are acrostics.

works.title: ISAIAH 40-55 (SECOND ISAIAH)
note: Anonymous, late exilic, addressed to deportees on the eve of Cyrus' victory, whom it names outright. Introduces the Servant figure of chapters 42, 49, 50, and 52-53.

positions.trad: Isaiah son of Amoz, writing prophetically of the exile
positions.tradWhy: Naming Cyrus before his birth is understood as genuine foreknowledge rather than evidence of a late writer.
positions.tradSource: Isaiah 44:28, 45:1; Isaiah 46:9-10 on declaring the end from the beginning
positions.crit: An anonymous prophet in Babylon, c. 550-540 BCE
positions.critWhy: It addresses exiles as a present audience and treats the rise of Cyrus as current events.
positions.critSource: Doderlein, 1775; Duhm, 1892

trad.basis: the first deportation to the edict of Cyrus

works.title: OBADIAH
note: The shortest book in the Hebrew Bible. Against Edom for its conduct at Jerusalem's fall, so most likely composed soon after 587 BCE.

sections.title: SECTION V.  EARLY POST-EXILIC / PERSIAN PERIOD
sections.name: EARLY POST-EXILIC / PERSIAN PERIOD
intro: Cyrus takes Babylon in 539 and permits return. The temple is rebuilt by 515. In this period the Torah is edited into something close to its present shape and becomes the constitutional document of the restored community.

works.title: ON THE PLACEMENT OF THE TORAH
note: Genesis through Numbers appear here because the critical consensus places the final redaction of the Pentateuch in the Persian period. The traditions inside them are far older: the poems of Section I sit inside Exodus and Numbers, the priestly legislation preserves pre-exilic temple practice, and the narrative sources are usually dated to the monarchy. Deuteronomy is in Section III with Josiah's reform. Readers who follow the traditional Mosaic dating should read Genesis through Deuteronomy first, before Section I.

works.title: GENESIS
note: Primeval history in chapters 1-11 and ancestral narratives in 12-50. Jubilees, in Section VII, is a rewriting of this book plus early Exodus.

positions.tradWhy: Jewish and Christian tradition ascribes the Torah to Moses. Later scripture speaks of 'the book of Moses', and Jesus refers to what Moses wrote.
positions.tradSource: Talmud, Bava Batra 14b-15a; 2 Chronicles 35:12; Mark 12:26; John 5:46-47
positions.crit: Composite; final form in the Persian period, c. 500-400 BCE
positions.critWhy: Doublets, two divine names, and differences of vocabulary and theology are read as evidence of combined sources. Genesis 14 and 36 mention kings and customs of later eras.
positions.critSource: Julius Wellhausen, Prolegomena to the History of Israel, 1878, building on Astruc 1753 and Graf 1866

works.title: EXODUS
note: Deliverance, covenant, law, and tabernacle. Chapter 15 is reproduced in Section I as one of the oldest units in the Bible.

positions.tradWhy: The book records Moses writing down what he was given.
positions.critWhy: The Song of the Sea in chapter 15 is archaic Hebrew, linguistically older than the prose around it, which is itself evidence the book gathers material of different ages.
positions.critSource: Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman, Studies in Ancient Yahwistic Poetry, 1950

crit.basis: the fall of Babylon to Alexander

works.title: LEVITICUS
note: Sacrificial and purity law. Chapters 17-26, the Holiness Code, are usually treated as a distinct block. The Temple Scroll from Qumran, summarized in Section VII, rewrites and expands this legislation.

positions.tradWhy: Framed throughout as speech of Yahweh to Moses.
positions.crit: Priestly source, exilic to Persian period
positions.critWhy: Its vocabulary and cultic concerns match the priestly material elsewhere in the Torah, associated with the Second Temple.
positions.critSource: Wellhausen, Prolegomena, 1878

crit.basis: the fall of Babylon to Alexander

works.title: NUMBERS
note: Wilderness narrative and law. Chapters 23-24 preserve the archaic Balaam oracles; 6:24-26 is the blessing found on the Ketef Hinnom amulets, reproduced in Section X.

positions.tradWhy: Traditional Mosaic authorship of the Torah as a whole.
positions.critWhy: Contains very old poetry, notably the Oracles of Balaam, inside a later narrative frame.
positions.critSource: William F. Albright, 'The Oracles of Balaam', Journal of Biblical Literature, 1944

crit.basis: the fall of Babylon to Alexander

works.title: HAGGAI
note: Precisely dated to 520 BCE. Urges the rebuilding of the temple.

works.title: ZECHARIAH 1-8
note: 520-518 BCE, contemporary with Haggai. Eight night visions supporting the rebuilding. Chapters 9-14 are later and appear in Section VI.

works.title: MALACHI
note: Mid-fifth century, after the temple is functioning again. Addresses priestly negligence, intermarriage, and divorce.

works.title: ISAIAH 56-66 (THIRD ISAIAH)
note: Post-exilic, addressed to a disappointing restored community rather than to exiles awaiting release.

positions.tradWhy: Part of the single scroll bearing his name.
positions.crit: Anonymous, after the return, c. 537-500 BCE
positions.critWhy: It presupposes a community back in the land with the temple in view.
positions.critSource: Duhm, 1892, who first separated these chapters

works.title: PSALMS
note: The Psalter as a collection reaches its final form in this period, but individual psalms range from the monarchy to the Hellenistic age, and the arrangement into five books is editorial. The Qumran psalms scrolls preserve a different order and additional compositions.

positions.trad: David wrote most, with Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon and Moses
positions.tradWhy: Seventy-three psalms carry Davidic superscriptions, and the apostles cite psalms as David's own words.
positions.crit: A collection spanning centuries, compiled by the Persian period
positions.critWhy: Some psalms presuppose the exile. The Hebrew preposition in the superscriptions can mean 'belonging to' or 'in the manner of' as readily as 'by'.
positions.critSource: Psalm 137:1; Hermann Gunkel, Einleitung in die Psalmen, 1933

crit.basis: the fall of Babylon to Alexander

works.title: PSALM 151
note: A short psalm on David's anointing, present in the Greek and Syriac Psalters and in Hebrew at Qumran, where it appears in an older and longer form. Included in Orthodox Bibles; not in Jewish, Protestant, or Catholic canons.

works.title: JOB
note: Date debated across several centuries. A prose frame around a long poetic dispute on innocent suffering and the limits of human understanding.

positions.trad: Moses, or an ancient author of the patriarchal era
positions.tradWhy: The Talmud suggests Moses. The setting has wealth counted in livestock, sacrifice offered by the head of the family, and no mention of Israel, the law or the temple.
positions.crit: 6th-4th century BCE, around an older folk tale
positions.critWhy: The prose frame and the poetic dialogue differ in style and outlook, and the Hebrew carries Aramaisms.
positions.critSource: Job 1-2 and 42:7-17 against 3:1-42:6; Marvin Pope, Job, Anchor Bible, 1965

works.title: PROVERBS
note: A compilation. Chapters 10-29 contain older material; chapters 1-9, the frame with personified Wisdom, are usually judged post-exilic. Compare Sirach and Wisdom of Solomon in Sections VII and VIII.

positions.tradWhy: The book opens in his name and Kings credits him with three thousand proverbs.
positions.crit: A compilation of several collections; final form post-exilic
positions.critWhy: The book names other authors within itself, and one collection is explicitly said to have been copied out by Hezekiah's men, some two and a half centuries after Solomon.

crit.basis: the return under Cyrus to Alexander

works.title: RUTH
note: Set in the period of the judges; date of composition disputed, with many placing it post-exilic as a counterweight to the marriage policies of Ezra-Nehemiah. In Jewish tradition it belongs to the Writings, not to the historical books.

positions.tradWhy: The Talmud assigns Ruth to Samuel; the story is set in the period of the judges.
positions.crit: Disputed; post-exilic on one reading, pre-exilic on another
positions.critWhy: Often read as a response to the post-exilic dissolution of foreign marriages, since its heroine is a Moabite ancestor of David. Against that, its Hebrew is classical rather than late.
positions.critSource: Ezra 10:10-11 for the setting proposed; on the classical Hebrew, Edward F. Campbell, Ruth, Anchor Bible, 1975

crit.basis: the return under Cyrus to Alexander

sections.title: SECTION VI.  LATER PERSIAN TO EARLY HELLENISTIC
sections.name: LATER PERSIAN TO EARLY HELLENISTIC
intro: Alexander's conquest in 332 replaces Persian rule with Greek. These works reflect life under empire, arguments about identity and intermarriage, wisdom pressed to its limits, and, at the end of the period, the earliest Jewish apocalyptic writing.

works.title: 1 CHRONICLES
note: A retelling of Israel's history from Adam to the exile, using Samuel-Kings as a source but rewriting it around David, the temple, and its liturgy.

positions.tradWhy: The Talmud assigns Chronicles to Ezra.
positions.critWhy: The genealogy of David's line runs several generations past the exile.
positions.critSource: 1 Chronicles 3:19-24; Sara Japhet, I and II Chronicles, 1993

works.title: 2 CHRONICLES
note: Continues to the fall of Jerusalem and the edict of Cyrus, which is also where Ezra begins.

positions.tradWhy: The Talmud assigns Chronicles to Ezra.
positions.critWhy: It ends mid-sentence with the decree of Cyrus, at precisely the point where Ezra begins.
positions.critSource: 2 Chronicles 36:22-23 against Ezra 1:1-3

works.title: EZRA
note: Return, temple rebuilding, and the reform of Ezra. Contains Aramaic documents. In the Hebrew tradition Ezra-Nehemiah is a single book.

works.title: NEHEMIAH
note: Rebuilding of the wall and community reform, partly in first-person memoir form.

works.title: ESTHER (HEBREW)
note: A diaspora court tale explaining Purim. Famously never names God. It is the only book of the Hebrew Bible with no copy among the Dead Sea Scrolls. The expanded Greek version follows in Section VII.

positions.tradWhy: The book records Mordecai writing these things down and sending letters.
positions.critWhy: Written to account for the origin of Purim, a festival with no basis in the Torah. God is never named in the book.
positions.critSource: Esther 9:26-28; Carey Moore, Esther, Anchor Bible, 1971

works.title: ECCLESIASTES
note: Qoheleth. Persian or early Hellenistic. Presses wisdom against the fact of death and finds it insufficient.

positions.tradWhy: The speaker calls himself son of David, king in Jerusalem.
positions.critWhy: Late Hebrew with Persian loanwords, and a speaker who looks back on kingship rather than exercising it.
positions.critSource: Persian 'pardes' at Ecclesiastes 2:5; Franz Delitzsch, 1875, who judged the language decisive against Solomonic authorship

works.title: SONG OF SONGS
note: Love poetry, later read allegorically in both Jewish and Christian tradition. Linguistic evidence points to a late date for the collection.

positions.tradWhy: Ascribed to Solomon in its opening line.
positions.crit: Genuinely unsettled, from the 10th to the 3rd century BCE
positions.critWhy: Persian loanwords point late; the poetry closely resembles much older Egyptian love song. Neither argument has carried the day.
positions.critSource: Persian 'pardes' at Song 4:13; Michael V. Fox, The Song of Songs and the Ancient Egyptian Love Songs, 1985

works.title: JONAH
note: A prophetic parable about divine mercy extended to Nineveh, rather than a collection of oracles.

positions.trad: Jonah son of Amittai, 8th century BCE
positions.tradWhy: It names the prophet known from the reign of Jeroboam II, and Jesus refers to the sign of Jonah.
positions.critWhy: Late Hebrew, Aramaic loanwords, and Nineveh described in the past tense as a city that was great.
positions.critSource: Jonah 3:3; Otto Eissfeldt, The Old Testament: An Introduction, 1934

works.title: JOEL
note: Locust plague and the day of the LORD. Date debated across several centuries; commonly placed in the Persian period.

positions.tradWhy: Its placement among the earlier of the Twelve was traditionally taken to imply an early date.
positions.tradSource: Position in the Masoretic order of the Twelve; Joel 1:1, which gives no king and so no fixed date
positions.critWhy: It assumes a functioning temple and no monarchy, and mentions Greeks as distant slave-traders.
positions.critSource: Joel 3:6; Hans Walter Wolff, Joel and Amos, 1969

works.title: ZECHARIAH 9-14
note: Anonymous later material appended to Zechariah, often assigned to the Hellenistic period. A major source of imagery in the Gospel passion narratives.

positions.tradWhy: Part of the single book bearing his name.
positions.critWhy: The book shifts from precisely dated oracles about rebuilding to undated apocalyptic, and Greece appears as a power.
positions.critSource: Zechariah 9:13; Joseph Mede, 1653, who first argued the division

works.title: 1 ENOCH: THE BOOK OF THE WATCHERS (chapters 1-36)
note: Third century BCE, and one of the earliest Jewish apocalyptic writings. Angels called Watchers descend, take human wives, teach metallurgy, cosmetics, sorcery, and astrology, and father the giant Nephilim; the earth cries out, the archangels intervene, and the Watchers are bound. Enoch is then taken on tours of the cosmos and shown the places of the dead, the mountains of judgment, and the tree of life. Aramaic fragments were found at Qumran. Quoted directly in Jude 14-15. Canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition; in no other major canon.

Translation: R. H. Charles, 1917. Charles used double square brackets for material he judged interpolated, single brackets for restorations, and parentheses for words supplied for sense; daggers mark corrupt text. These marks are preserved as printed.

positions.trad: Enoch, seventh from Adam, before the flood
positions.tradWhy: The book claims Enoch as its author, and Jude quotes it as prophecy from Enoch, the seventh from Adam. It is canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.
positions.tradSource: 1 Enoch 1:1-2 and Jude 14-15, both in this volume
positions.critWhy: Aramaic fragments at Qumran place it among the earliest Jewish apocalyptic writing.
positions.critSource: 4QEn-a (Qumran); J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch, 1976

works.title: 1 ENOCH: THE ASTRONOMICAL BOOK (chapters 72-82)
note: Third century BCE or earlier, and possibly the oldest section of 1 Enoch. Presents the movements of sun, moon, stars, and winds as fixed law, and defends a 364-day solar calendar against a lunar reckoning. The same calendar drives Jubilees and the Qumran community's festival practice, which is why calendar disputes matter so much in Section VII. Placed here out of numerical order because of its early date; chapters 37-71 and 83-108 follow in Sections VII and VIII.

works.title: TOBIT
note: c. 225-175 BCE. A didactic story set in the Assyrian exile. Tobit goes blind after burying the dead in defiance of the king; his son Tobias travels with the angel Raphael in disguise, recovers a debt, marries Sarah after driving off the demon Asmodeus, and returns to heal his father. Themes: almsgiving, burial of the dead, endogamy, angelic guidance, providence. Aramaic and Hebrew fragments were found at Qumran. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; not in Jewish or Protestant canons.

sections.title: SECTION VII.  HIGH HELLENISTIC AND MACCABEAN PERIOD
sections.name: HIGH HELLENISTIC AND MACCABEAN PERIOD
intro: Seleucid rule, the persecution under Antiochus IV, the Maccabean revolt of 167-164, and the Hasmonean state that follows. This is the most productive century in the whole collection: wisdom literature, rewritten scripture, apocalypse, history, and the sectarian library at Qumran all belong here.

works.title: SIRACH (ECCLESIASTICUS)
note: Hebrew original c. 180-175 BCE by Jesus ben Sira of Jerusalem, translated into Greek by his grandson, who explains the circumstances in a prologue. Practical wisdom on speech, money, friendship, family, and the fear of the Lord, closing with the Praise of the Ancestors in chapters 44-50. Substantial portions of the lost Hebrew original were recovered from the Cairo Genizah and at Masada. In Catholic and Orthodox canons; not in Jewish or Protestant canons.

works.title: JUBILEES
note: Mid-second century BCE. A retelling of Genesis and Exodus 1-14 presented as revelation dictated to Moses on Sinai by the angel of the presence, with all events dated by jubilee periods of forty-nine years. It insists on a 364-day solar calendar, hardens Sabbath and festival law, backdates the festivals to the patriarchs, and sharpens the separation of Israel from the nations. Angels and the demonic prince Mastema act throughout. About fifteen copies were found at Qumran, more than most biblical books. Canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition; in no other major canon.
Translation: R. H. Charles, 1917, from the Ethiopic. Daggers mark readings Charles judged corrupt; brackets mark restorations.

positions.trad: Revelation given to Moses at Sinai
positions.tradWhy: The book presents itself as dictated to Moses by an angel of the presence. It is canonical scripture in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.
positions.tradSource: Jubilees, Prologue and 1:27, in this volume
positions.critWhy: Its 364-day solar calendar and priestly preoccupations fit the Maccabean era, and Hebrew fragments were found at Qumran.
positions.critSource: Jubilees 6:32-38, in this volume; 4Q216-4Q228 (Qumran); James VanderKam, The Book of Jubilees, 2001

works.title: DANIEL
note: Reaches its present form c. 165 BCE, during the persecution under Antiochus IV, though the court tales in chapters 1-6 are older. Chapters 7-12 are apocalyptic visions that read the history of empires forward to the end of that persecution and close with the earliest unambiguous statement of resurrection in the Hebrew Bible. Written partly in Hebrew and partly in Aramaic. Canonical everywhere; the Greek additions follow.

positions.trad: Daniel, 6th century BCE, in Babylon and Persia
positions.tradWhy: The book presents itself as Daniel's, set in the exile, and Jesus refers to it as the work of 'the prophet Daniel'.
positions.crit: c. 165 BCE, during the Maccabean crisis
positions.critWhy: Chapter 11 tracks Hellenistic dynastic politics in detail up to Antiochus IV, then its account of his death diverges from what happened, which places the writer at that moment.
positions.critSource: Porphyry, 3rd century, preserved in Jerome's Commentary on Daniel; the divergence is at Daniel 11:40-45

works.title: THE PRAYER OF AZARIAH AND THE SONG OF THE THREE (Greek Daniel 3:24-90)
note: One of three Greek additions to Daniel. Inserted into the furnace scene: a penitential prayer and a hymn of the whole creation, the latter familiar in Christian liturgy as the Benedicite. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

works.title: SUSANNA (Greek Daniel 13)
note: Two elders extort a virtuous woman and perjure themselves; the young Daniel cross-examines them separately and their stories disagree. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

works.title: BEL AND THE DRAGON (Greek Daniel 14)
note: Two satirical tales against idolatry, in which Daniel exposes the priests of Bel by dusting the temple floor with ash and kills a venerated serpent. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

works.title: JUDITH
note: A pious widow talks her way into the enemy camp and beheads the general Holofernes in his tent. Deliberately unhistorical in its setting, which is signaled from the opening verse. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; not in Jewish or Protestant canons.

works.title: BARUCH
note: Attributed to Jeremiah's secretary. A confession of national sin, a poem on wisdom as Torah, and consolation addressed to Jerusalem. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

works.title: THE LETTER OF JEREMIAH (Baruch 6)
note: A separate work, printed as Baruch 6 in most Bibles and as its own book in Orthodox ones. A sustained satire on the powerlessness of idols. A Greek fragment was found at Qumran.

works.title: 1 MACCABEES
note: A sober dynastic history of the revolt from the persecution of 167 BCE through the consolidation of Hasmonean rule, written in support of that dynasty. Composed in Hebrew, surviving in Greek. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

works.title: 2 MACCABEES
note: Not a sequel but an independent condensation of a five-volume work by Jason of Cyrene, covering a shorter span with a heavier theological hand: martyrdom, bodily resurrection, creation out of nothing, and prayer for the dead. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

works.title: ESTHER, GREEK VERSION
note: The Greek Esther is roughly a sixth longer than the Hebrew, adding six large passages conventionally lettered A-F: Mordecai's dream and its interpretation, the texts of the royal decrees, and prayers by Mordecai and Esther. The additions supply the explicit references to God that the Hebrew book lacks. Printed here in full, so the Hebrew book in Section VI and this version can be compared. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

works.title: 1 ESDRAS
note: A Greek reworking covering material from 2 Chronicles 35 through Nehemiah 8, with a different sequence of events and one large original episode: the contest of the three bodyguards over what is strongest, won by the argument that truth is. Canonical in Orthodox Bibles; in an appendix in Catholic tradition.

works.title: THE PRAYER OF MANASSEH
note: A short penitential prayer put in the mouth of the worst king in Chronicles, supplying the prayer that 2 Chronicles 33:18-19 mentions but does not quote. Canonical in Orthodox Bibles; in an appendix in Catholic tradition.

works.title: 1 ENOCH: DREAM VISIONS AND THE EPISTLE OF ENOCH (chapters 83-108)
note: Second century BCE. Chapters 83-90 contain the Animal Apocalypse, which retells all of Israel's history with the actors as animals and ends in the Maccabean crisis, allowing a reasonably firm date. Chapters 91-108, the Epistle of Enoch, include the Apocalypse of Weeks, which divides history into ten weeks, and a series of woes against the rich and the oppressor. Translation: R. H. Charles, 1917.

works.title: THE MAJOR DEAD SEA SCROLLS: SUMMARIES
note: About 900 to 1,000 manuscripts were recovered from eleven caves near Qumran between 1947 and 1956. Roughly a quarter are biblical; the rest are previously unknown works. Together they describe a movement, usually identified with the Essenes, that regarded itself as the true remnant of Israel, followed a stricter interpretation of the law than the Jerusalem establishment, kept a 364-day solar calendar, rejected the current temple administration, and expected an imminent final war and purification.

A NOTE ON WHY THE TEXTS THEMSELVES ARE NOT PRINTED HERE. Every complete English translation of the non-biblical scrolls was made in the twentieth or twenty-first century and is under active copyright: Vermes, Wise-Abegg-Cook, Garcia Martinez-Tigchelaar, and the Discoveries in the Judaean Desert volumes. Unlike the King James Version, the World English Bible, or the Charles translations used elsewhere in this volume, none of them can be reproduced. What follows is descriptive summary only. For the texts, the standard one-volume options are Vermes, The Complete Dead Sea Scrolls in English, and Wise, Abegg and Cook, The Dead Sea Scrolls: A New Translation. Photographs and transcriptions of many scrolls are freely viewable through the Israel Antiquities Authority's Leon Levy Digital Library and the Israel Museum's Digital Dead Sea Scrolls.

COMMUNITY RULE (1QS, Serekh ha-Yahad). The central rule book. Covers admission through a multi- year probation, the annual covenant renewal ceremony, the ranked structure of the community, common property, pure meals, and a detailed penal code with penalties for lying about property, interrupting, sleeping in session, and spitting in the assembly. Its theological core is the Treatise of the Two Spirits: God created two spirits, of light and darkness, that struggle within every person until the appointed end.

DAMASCUS DOCUMENT (CD, plus Qumran copies). Known first from two medieval copies found in the Cairo Genizah in 1896, half a century before the caves. Opens with a historical review of a remnant that God raised up after the exile and a Teacher of Righteousness sent to guide it, and warns against a figure called the Scoffer or the Man of the Lie. Its legal half covers Sabbath restrictions, oaths, purity, marriage, and dealings with outsiders. It legislates for members living in towns with wives and children, so it describes a broader movement than the celibate- looking community of 1QS.

WAR SCROLL (1QM). A manual for the final forty-year war between the Sons of Light and the Sons of Darkness, the latter led by the Kittim, most likely the Romans. Specifies trumpet calls, banner inscriptions, troop formations, cavalry, the ages of combatants, priestly conduct, and the prayers to be recited. The battle swings back and forth in seven lots until God intervenes directly.

THANKSGIVING HYMNS (Hodayot, 1QH). Some twenty-five to thirty poems in the first person, each typically opening with thanks to God. Recurring themes: human nothingness and impurity, election by grace, revelation of hidden mysteries, betrayal by former friends, and rescue from enemies. A subset, the so-called Teacher Hymns, are often read as the voice of the Teacher of Righteousness himself.

PESHARIM (continuous commentaries). Verse-by-verse commentaries on prophetic books, most fully preserved for Habakkuk, Nahum, and Psalms. Each quotes a lemma and then decodes it as a prediction of the community's own recent history, its Teacher, and its opponents: the Wicked Priest, the Man of the Lie, and the Kittim. The Nahum pesher is unusual in naming Demetrius and Antiochus outright and in describing men hanged alive. These are the earliest known continuous biblical commentaries.

TEMPLE SCROLL (11QT). At over eight meters, the longest scroll found. Rewrites the law of Deuteronomy and the priestly legislation as first-person divine speech, removing the mediating voice of Moses. Contains a vast idealized temple plan with three concentric courts, a festival calendar with additional first-fruits festivals, purity rules for the city, and a law of the king restricting his army, wives, and wealth.

MIQSAT MA'ASE HA-TORAH (4QMMT). A letter-like text listing roughly twenty points of legal disagreement over sacrifice, purity, and marriage, addressed to a leader in terms that are firm but not hostile. Frequently read as an early document from the separation itself.

OTHER MATERIAL. The Genesis Apocryphon, an Aramaic expansion of Genesis; the Copper Scroll, an inventory of buried treasure incised on metal; the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice, a liturgical cycle of angelic worship; 4QInstruction, a long wisdom text; the New Jerusalem text; calendrical rosters of priestly courses; horoscopes; and Aramaic works related to Enoch, Levi, and Daniel.

sections.title: SECTION VIII.  LATE HELLENISTIC TO EARLY ROMAN
sections.name: LATE HELLENISTIC TO EARLY ROMAN
intro: Pompey takes Jerusalem in 63 BCE and Judea passes under Roman control. Greek-speaking Judaism in Alexandria produces philosophically ambitious writing, while in Judea the loss of independence generates fresh messianic expectation.

works.title: THE WISDOM OF SOLOMON
note: Composed in Greek, most likely in Alexandria, late first century BCE or early first century CE. Argues that the righteous are immortal and that death entered through envy, personifies Wisdom in strongly philosophical language, mocks idolatry at length, and rereads the Exodus plagues as a demonstration that creation itself fights for the just. Its vocabulary influenced early Christian writing considerably. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

works.title: 1 ENOCH: THE BOOK OF PARABLES (chapters 37-71)
note: Three parables on the coming judgment, dated by most scholars to the late first century BCE or the first century CE, later than the rest of 1 Enoch. This is the section that develops the figure called the Son of Man, the Elect One, and the Righteous One, who sits on a throne of glory to judge kings and the mighty. Notably, it is the only major section of 1 Enoch with no identified fragment among the Dead Sea Scrolls, which is central to the argument for its later date. Translation: R. H. Charles, 1917.

works.title: THE PSALMS OF SOLOMON
note: Eighteen psalms, composed in Hebrew in the mid-first century BCE and surviving in Greek and Syriac, written from a circle sharply critical of the Hasmonean rulers. Psalms 2, 8, and 17 respond directly to Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BCE, which they read as divine punishment of illegitimate priest-kings, and to Pompey's own death in Egypt in 48. Psalm 17 is the most important single text: it prays for a Davidic king, called there the Lord Messiah, who will purge Jerusalem of foreign rulers, gather the tribes, judge with wisdom, and rule without relying on horse or army. It is the fullest pre-Christian portrait of a Davidic messiah that survives. In no canon, though it appears in the table of contents of the fifth-century Codex Alexandrinus.

Text not reproduced here: the accessible modern English translations are in copyright, and the public domain versions of Ryle and James (1891) and Gray (1913) exist only as page scans interleaved with Greek text and commentary, which cannot be extracted cleanly. Both are freely readable at archive.org.

works.title: 3 MACCABEES
note: First century BCE, from Egypt. Despite the name, it concerns neither the Maccabees nor the Seleucids: Ptolemy IV, thwarted at the Jerusalem temple, orders the Jews of Egypt trampled by drunken elephants, and the plan collapses. Canonical in Orthodox Bibles.

works.title: 4 MACCABEES
note: First century CE. A philosophical treatise arguing that devout reason masters the passions, proved from the martyrdoms of Eleazar and the mother with seven sons taken from 2 Maccabees. Stoic in vocabulary, Jewish in commitment. In an appendix to the Greek Bible; not canonical in the Western churches.

works.title: PHILO OF ALEXANDRIA
note: c. 20 BCE to c. 50 CE. The most prolific Jewish author of the period and a wealthy leader of the Alexandrian community, who led the embassy to Caligula in 39-40 CE. His surviving work runs to dozens of treatises reading the Torah allegorically through Middle Platonic and Stoic philosophy, in which Abraham's journey becomes the soul's ascent and the literal sense, which Philo insists must still be observed, carries a philosophical meaning beneath it. His use of the Logos as the intermediary through which God acts on the world had considerable influence on later Christian theology. Not scripture in any tradition and not reproduced here on grounds of length; the complete Yonge translation of 1854-1855 is in the public domain and freely available.

sections.title: SECTION IX.  NEW TESTAMENT WRITINGS
sections.name: NEW TESTAMENT WRITINGS
intro: Arranged in approximate order of composition rather than canonical order, which is why the letters come before the Gospels. Dating is contested at almost every point; the sequence below reflects the mainstream range. The seven letters generally accepted as Paul's own come first, then those whose authorship is disputed, then the Gospels in the order most commonly reconstructed, then the remaining letters and Revelation.

works.title: 1 THESSALONIANS
note: c. 50 CE. The earliest surviving Christian document of any kind.

works.title: GALATIANS
note: c. 50-55 CE. The sharpest statement of Paul's position on law and gentile inclusion.

works.title: 1 CORINTHIANS
note: c. 53-55 CE. Answers to a specific congregation's disputes; preserves the earliest account of the resurrection tradition in chapter 15.

works.title: 2 CORINTHIANS
note: c. 55-56 CE. Possibly a composite of more than one letter.

works.title: ROMANS
note: c. 56-58 CE. The longest and most systematic of Paul's letters, written to a church he had not founded.

works.title: PHILIPPIANS
note: c. 55-62 CE, from prison. Contains the early hymn of chapter 2.

works.title: PHILEMON
note: c. 55-62 CE. A private note about the slave Onesimus; the shortest of Paul's letters.

works.title: COLOSSIANS
note: c. 60-80 CE. Authorship disputed.

positions.tradWhy: Names Paul and Timothy, and its personal greetings match those of Philemon, a letter nobody disputes.
positions.crit: Disputed; Paul or a close follower, c. 60-80 CE
positions.critWhy: Style and a more cosmic Christology than the undisputed letters, though the personal detail is hard to explain as invention.
positions.critSource: Colossians 1:15-20; Eduard Lohse, Colossians and Philemon, 1971

works.title: EPHESIANS
note: c. 80-95 CE. Widely, though not universally, regarded as written in Paul's name after his death.

positions.tradWhy: The letter names Paul as its author twice.
positions.crit: A follower of Paul, c. 80-100 CE
positions.critWhy: Its vocabulary and very long sentences differ from the undisputed letters, and it runs closely parallel to Colossians throughout.
positions.critSource: Ephesians 6:21-22 against Colossians 4:7-8; Edgar Goodspeed, The Meaning of Ephesians, 1933

works.title: 2 THESSALONIANS
note: Date and authorship disputed; either c. 51 CE or considerably later.

positions.tradWhy: Names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, as does the first letter.
positions.critWhy: Its sequence of end-time events is hard to square with the first letter's thief in the night, and it warns readers against letters forged in Paul's name.
positions.critSource: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-4 against 1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:2, 3:17

works.title: 1 TIMOTHY
note: The Pastoral Epistles, c. 90-110 CE by most reckonings, addressed to church order and succession.

positions.trad: Paul, c. 62-64 CE, after release from a first Roman imprisonment
positions.tradWhy: Names Paul, and assumes travels not recorded in Acts, which tradition explains by a later missionary period.
positions.tradSource: 1 Timothy 1:1, 1:3; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.22, on a release and second imprisonment
positions.crit: A follower of Paul, c. 90-110 CE
positions.critWhy: The three Pastorals share a vocabulary unlike Paul's and address a settled church order of overseers and deacons.
positions.critSource: 1 Timothy 3:1-13; Friedrich Schleiermacher, 1807; P. N. Harrison, The Problem of the Pastoral Epistles, 1921

works.title: 2 TIMOTHY
note: Pastoral Epistle.

positions.trad: Paul, c. 64-67 CE, shortly before his execution
positions.tradWhy: Reads as a farewell, and is the most personal of the three.
positions.crit: A follower of Paul, c. 90-110 CE
positions.critWhy: Grouped with the other Pastorals on shared vocabulary and style.
positions.critSource: Harrison, 1921

works.title: TITUS
note: Pastoral Epistle.

positions.tradWhy: Names Paul, and assumes a mission in Crete.
positions.crit: A follower of Paul, c. 90-110 CE
positions.critWhy: Grouped with the other Pastorals on shared vocabulary and church order.
positions.critSource: Titus 1:5-9; Harrison, 1921

works.title: JAMES
note: Date ranges widely, from the 50s to the early second century. Wisdom instruction in the manner of Sirach rather than a letter of argument.

positions.trad: James the brother of Jesus, before 62 CE
positions.tradWhy: Attributed to James, leader of the Jerusalem church, whose death Eusebius places in the early 60s.
positions.critWhy: Its polished Greek is unexpected from a Galilean, and its treatment of faith and works is read by some as answering Paul, which would require a later date.
positions.critSource: James 2:14-26 against Romans 3:28; Martin Dibelius, Der Brief des Jakobus, 1921

works.title: MARK
note: c. 65-70 CE, around the Jewish revolt. Generally held to be the earliest Gospel and a source for Matthew and Luke.

positions.trad: Mark, recording Peter's preaching, c. 50s-60s CE
positions.tradWhy: Papias states that Mark was Peter's interpreter and wrote down accurately, though not in order, what Peter taught.
positions.tradSource: Papias, in this volume, Fragment VI; via Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.15
positions.crit: Anonymous, c. 65-75 CE; the earliest of the gospels
positions.critWhy: Its priority is broadly agreed, and chapter 13 suggests the Jewish revolt is under way or just past.
positions.critSource: Mark 13:1-2, 13:14; Lachmann, 1835; H. J. Holtzmann, 1863

works.title: MATTHEW
note: c. 80-90 CE. Uses Mark, adds a large body of teaching, and presents Jesus in continuity with Moses and the prophets.

positions.tradWhy: Papias, writing within living memory, reports that Matthew compiled the sayings in the Hebrew tongue.
positions.tradSource: Papias, in this volume, Fragment VI; via Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.16
positions.critWhy: It reproduces about ninety per cent of Mark, which an eyewitness apostle would have little need to do, and its parable of the burned city is widely read as knowing of Jerusalem's fall in 70.
positions.critSource: Matthew 22:7; on Markan priority, Karl Lachmann, 1835

works.title: LUKE
note: c. 80-90 CE. Volume one of a two-part work addressed to Theophilus.

positions.trad: Luke the physician, Paul's companion, c. 60-62 CE
positions.tradWhy: Irenaeus names Luke as the author. The narrative of Acts switches to the first person during the voyages, implying a travelling companion, and it ends with Paul still alive.
positions.critWhy: It depends on Mark, and its version of the Olivet discourse describes an army encircling Jerusalem, read as the siege of 70 in retrospect.
positions.critSource: Luke 21:20 against Mark 13:14; Lachmann, 1835

works.title: ACTS
note: c. 80-90 CE. Volume two, carrying the movement from Jerusalem to Rome.

positions.tradWhy: Same author as the gospel, addressed to the same patron, and it breaks off with Paul under house arrest rather than recording his death.
positions.critWhy: It follows the gospel of Luke, which is itself dated after Mark.
positions.critSource: Acts 1:1; Henry Cadbury, The Making of Luke-Acts, 1927

works.title: JOHN
note: c. 90-100 CE. Independent of the other three in structure, chronology, and idiom.

positions.trad: John the apostle, son of Zebedee, c. 90 CE
positions.tradWhy: Irenaeus names John, the disciple who leaned on the Lord's breast, publishing the gospel at Ephesus, and the book itself claims eyewitness testimony.
positions.critWhy: Chapter 21 reads as an appendix after a formal ending, and the language about being put out of the synagogue suits a later setting than the ministry it narrates.
positions.critSource: John 20:30-31 followed by chapter 21; John 9:22, 16:2; J. Louis Martyn, History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel, 1968

works.title: HEBREWS
note: c. 60-90 CE. Anonymous. A sustained argument that the priesthood of Christ supersedes the temple system, drawing heavily on Leviticus and Psalms.

positions.trad: Paul, or Barnabas, Apollos or Luke
positions.tradWhy: It circulated among the Pauline letters in the East, which helped secure its place in the canon, though its authorship was argued over from the start.
positions.tradSource: P46, c. 200, which places Hebrews among Paul's letters; Tertullian, On Modesty 20, proposing Barnabas
positions.critWhy: The letter never names its author, and Origen said outright that only God knows who wrote it.
positions.critSource: Origen, quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 6.25.14

works.title: 1 PETER
note: c. 70-90 CE. Addressed to scattered congregations in Asia Minor under social pressure.

positions.tradWhy: Names Peter, and names Silvanus as the hand that wrote it, which accounts for the polished Greek.
positions.crit: Disputed; Peter or a follower, c. 70-90 CE
positions.critWhy: It addresses persecution across Asia Minor, and its use of 'Babylon' for Rome is characteristic of the period after 70 CE.
positions.critSource: 1 Peter 5:13; compare Revelation 17:5 and 2 Esdras 3:1-2, both in this volume

works.title: JUDE
note: c. 70-100 CE. Quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 directly in verses 14-15 and alludes to the Watchers tradition, making it the clearest canonical link to the literature in Sections VI and VII.

positions.trad: Jude the brother of James, c. 60-65 CE
positions.tradWhy: Names itself as from Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James.
positions.critWhy: It quotes 1 Enoch as prophecy, which shows how wide the range of authoritative writing still was.
positions.critSource: Jude 14-15 quoting 1 Enoch 1:9, both in this volume

works.title: REVELATION
note: c. 90-96 CE, most likely under Domitian. The one full apocalypse in the New Testament, dense with Daniel, Ezekiel, and Exodus imagery.

positions.trad: John the apostle, c. 95 CE, on Patmos
positions.tradWhy: Irenaeus places the vision at the end of Domitian's reign and identifies its author with the apostle.
positions.crit: John of Patmos, a different John, c. 95 CE
positions.critWhy: The date is broadly agreed. The Greek differs so sharply from the gospel of John that common authorship is doubted, an objection raised as early as the third century.
positions.critSource: Dionysius of Alexandria, quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 7.25

works.title: 2 PETER
note: c. 100-125 CE. Usually judged the latest writing in the New Testament. Reuses most of Jude and refers to a collection of Paul's letters as already established.

works.title: 2 ESDRAS (4 EZRA)
note: The Jewish core, chapters 3-14, was written c. 100 CE in response to the destruction of the temple in 70, and takes the form of seven dialogues in which Ezra presses an angel on why God permits the suffering of his own people. Chapters 1-2 and 15-16 are later Christian additions. Placed here because of its date, not because it is a New Testament book: it is canonical in Orthodox and Ethiopian traditions and printed in a Catholic appendix, but stands outside the Jewish and Protestant canons.

works.title: THE REST OF THE WORDS OF BARUCH
note: 4 Baruch, the Paraleipomena Jeremiou, which the Ethiopian canon receives as The Rest of the Words of Baruch. Jerusalem falls, Jeremiah goes into exile with the people, and Abimelech the Ethiopian sleeps sixty-six years under a tree with a basket of figs that do not spoil.

This is not the Ge'ez. No public-domain English translation of the Ge'ez exists — the standard modern one is in copyright, and Rendel Harris's 1889 edition, the earliest in English, prints the Greek text with a study of it and translates nothing. What is printed here is the Armenian recension, in the English Issaverdens published at Venice in 1901, and it is the one he says was made from the Greek that the Ge'ez also descends from. It is a witness to this work in another version, which is a different thing from the version the Ethiopian church reads, and saying so is the point of this paragraph.

Issaverdens prints no chapter divisions, so this volume adds none. The nine chapters the work is usually cited by belong to the Greek text; ruling them onto a different recension by matching what looked like the right sentence would be an editorial claim wearing the clothes of a transcription.

sections.title: SECTION X.  DISCOVERIES THAT ILLUMINATE THE TEXT
sections.name: DISCOVERIES THAT ILLUMINATE THE TEXT
intro: Four finds changed what can be known about how these texts were transmitted. The passages they physically preserve are reproduced here so the evidence can be read against the text.

works.title: KETEF HINNOM SILVER SCROLLS (found 1979)
note: Two rolled silver amulets, the larger about the size of a thumb, excavated from a burial chamber on the shoulder of the Hinnom Valley in Jerusalem and dated to roughly 600 BCE, before the exile. Unrolling them took three years. They carry a version of the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26. They are the oldest physical fragments of any biblical text yet found, older than the Dead Sea Scrolls by about four centuries, and they establish that at least this formula was in circulation in written form in the First Temple period. The text as it stands in Numbers follows.

works.title: NUMBERS 6 (the priestly blessing is verses 24-26)
note: Reproduced here for comparison with the Ketef Hinnom amulets. The amulets' wording is close but not identical to the Masoretic text and includes additional lines.

works.title: THE DEAD SEA SCROLLS AS BIBLICAL MANUSCRIPTS (found 1947-1956)
note: Beyond the sectarian works summarized in Section VII, the caves held about 220 to 230 biblical manuscripts, including at least a fragment of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Cave 1 is nearly complete, over seven meters long, and dates to about 125 BCE. Before 1947 the oldest substantially complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts were medieval, the Aleppo Codex of about 930 CE and the Leningrad Codex of 1008 CE; the scrolls pushed the evidence back more than a thousand years. Their combined testimony is double-edged and both halves matter: many manuscripts are remarkably close to the medieval consonantal text, while others preserve genuinely different editions, some agreeing with the Greek Septuagint or the Samaritan Pentateuch against it. Textual standardization, in other words, came after this period rather than before it.

works.title: THE NASH PAPYRUS (acquired 1898-1903)
note: A single damaged sheet from Egypt, dated to roughly 150-100 BCE, carrying the Ten Commandments followed immediately by the Shema. Until the Dead Sea discoveries it was the oldest known Hebrew biblical manuscript by a wide margin. Its Decalogue mixes the Exodus and Deuteronomy wordings and its sequence matches a liturgical order attested in rabbinic sources, so it is usually taken to be a devotional or teaching text rather than a scroll of scripture. Both passages it preserves follow.

works.title: DEUTERONOMY 5 (the Decalogue)
note: Compare Exodus 20. The Nash Papyrus blends the two versions.

works.title: DEUTERONOMY 6 (the Shema is verses 4-9)
note: Follows the Decalogue directly on the Nash Papyrus.

works.title: THE GREAT CHRISTIAN CODICES
note: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century, are the oldest substantially complete Greek Bibles. Sinaiticus was identified at St Catherine's Monastery on Sinai by Constantin von Tischendorf in 1844 and 1859, and is now split across four institutions; it is fully digitized and freely readable online. Its contents are worth noting for canon history: it includes the Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas within the New Testament, and its Old Testament carries books that later canons divided over. Vaticanus has been in the Vatican Library since at least 1475. Together with the papyri, they are the basis of the modern critical Greek text.

Twelve deathbed addresses, one from each son of Jacob, each recalling the patriarch's own life and drawing a moral from it. Composed in Greek, probably second century BCE, carrying later Christian interpolations. Aramaic and Hebrew fragments of Levi and Naphtali were recovered at Qumran, placing part of this tradition well before the Christian era.

intro: Roberts-Donaldson translation, 1885. Public domain. Source: earlychristianwritings.com, shorter (genuine) recension.

Seven letters written about 107-110 CE by the bishop of Antioch while under military guard on the road to Rome and his execution. They are the earliest evidence for a single bishop leading each local church, and in Romans he begs the Christians there not to intervene to save him.

These letters survive in a shorter and a longer recension. The longer is a fourth-century expansion carrying interpolations; the shorter, given here, is the text accepted as genuine. Eight further letters bearing his name are later forgeries and are not included.

sections.title: APPENDIX A.  CANON COMPARISON
sections.name: APPENDIX A.  CANON COMPARISON
intro: JEWISH (TANAKH, 24 books). The same content as the 39-book Protestant Old Testament, counted and ordered differently: Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and Ezra-Nehemiah are one book each, the twelve minor prophets are one book, and the order runs Torah, Prophets, Writings, ending with Chronicles rather than Malachi.

PROTESTANT (66). The Tanakh's content plus the 27 New Testament books. The deuterocanonical books were printed in a separate Apocrypha section in the 1611 King James Bible and in most English Bibles until the nineteenth century, when Bible societies began omitting them.

CATHOLIC (73). Adds Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch with the Letter of Jeremiah, 1 and 2 Maccabees, and the Greek additions to Esther and Daniel. Fixed at the Council of Trent in 1546. 1 Esdras, 2 Esdras, and the Prayer of Manasseh are printed in an appendix, outside the canon.

EASTERN ORTHODOX. The Catholic list plus 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, and Psalm 151, with 4 Maccabees in an appendix. The Slavonic tradition also includes 2 Esdras. Greek Orthodox usage speaks of anagignoskomena, books that are read, rather than a sharp canonical boundary.

ETHIOPIAN ORTHODOX TEWAHEDO. The widest canon of any church, and the only one that includes 1 Enoch and Jubilees as scripture, alongside further works such as 4 Baruch and the Ethiopic Clement. Counts are given as 81 books, though the enumeration varies between lists.
Every book in every one of these canons is printed in full in this volume.

Chronological framework: adapted from the uploaded study guide, with the section structure and date ranges retained. Orientation notes, canon comparisons, scroll summaries, and editorial apparatus were written for this volume.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS. The Charles texts were digitized from print by optical character recognition and lightly hand-corrected; scattered typographic artifacts survive, and in the source edition the headings for 1 Enoch 78 and 102 are absent, with their text running on under the preceding chapter. Verse numbering in Jubilees follows the marginal numbering of the 1917 printing, which occasionally falls mid-sentence. The World English Bible text is clean and versified throughout.

web.label: World English Bible with Deuterocanon
web.detail: Published by eBible.org and dedicated to the public domain. A modern revision of the American Standard Version of 1901, rendering the divine name as Yahweh.

charles.label: R. H. Charles, 1917
charles.detail: Translated for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge and public domain by age. Double brackets mark words Charles restored by conjecture and a dagger marks a reading he judged corrupt. Verse numbers follow the marginal numbering of that printing and sometimes fall mid-sentence. The text was digitised by optical character recognition, so scattered typographic artifacts survive.

anf.label: Ante-Nicene Fathers, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885
anf.detail: Public domain by age. The Ignatian letters follow the shorter recension, the seven letters generally accepted as genuine. These texts carry no verse numbers in the original; chapter divisions are the editors'.

editorial.label: Editorial summary
editorial.detail: Written for this volume. No primary text was available from a public-domain source.

platt.label: Thomas Pell Platt, Oriental Translation Fund, 1834
platt.detail: Public domain by age, recovered from the scan of a facing-page printing of the Ge'ez with Platt's English beside it. Not audited: no independent reference counts exist for this text, so there is nothing to check it against but the scan.

horner.label: The Rev. G. Horner, The Statutes of the Apostles, 1904
horner.detail: Public domain by age. Horner's English of the Ge'ez Sinodos he prints in the same volume, recovered from the scan by the word coordinates rather than by its plain OCR. Not audited: no independent reference counts exist for this text. His own numbering is kept, including the two statutes he numbers 40.

issaverdens.label: Jacques Issaverdens, Venice, 1901
issaverdens.detail: Public domain by age. The Armenian recension made from the Greek, in Issaverdens's English, recovered from the scan by the word coordinates. It is a witness to the work the Ethiopian canon receives, not to the Ge'ez text of it, and no public-domain English of the Ge'ez exists. Not audited.

schodde.label: George H. Schodde, Journal of the Society of Biblical Literature and Exegesis, 1885
schodde.detail: Public domain by age. Schodde's English of the Ge'ez Apostolic Canons, recovered from the scan by the word coordinates. His roman numbering is the one printed; two of his headings did not survive the scan and their canons read on inside the canon before them. Not audited.

cooper.label: James Cooper and Arthur John Maclean, Edinburgh, 1902
cooper.detail: Public domain by age. The Testamentum Domini from the Syriac, recovered from the scan by the word coordinates. This is not the Ge'ez: the Ethiopic version of this work was unpublished when they wrote and has no public-domain English still. Their chapter numbers are the ones printed. Not audited.

james.label: Montague Rhodes James, The Apocryphal New Testament, 1924
james.detail: Public domain by age. James's English of the Ethiopic published by Guerrier, recovered from the scan by the word coordinates. His section numbers are the ones printed. Not audited.
